subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statement best describes destructive waves?
options: Low frequency waves with a strong swash and weak backwash that build up beaches
High frequency waves with a strong backwash and weak swash that erode beaches
Waves that only occur during calm summer conditions
Waves that carry sediment only by the process of solution
questions.explain: Destructive waves are high-energy, high-frequency waves whose strong backwash drags material back out to sea, eroding the beach.

questions.q: Why does longshore drift move sediment along a coastline in a zig-zag pattern?
options: Swash carries material straight up the beach while backwash pulls it back at an angle
Swash carries material up the beach at the angle of the wind while backwash returns it straight down under gravity
Tides push material along the beach twice each day
Wind blows the sediment directly along the top of the beach
questions.explain: The swash approaches at the angle of the prevailing wind but the backwash runs straight back down the slope under gravity, producing net movement along the coast.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence in the formation of coastal features from a crack in a headland?
options: Cave, arch, stack, stump
Stack, arch, cave, stump
Arch, cave, stump, stack
Cave, stack, arch, stump
questions.explain: Erosion widens a crack into a cave, then an arch through the headland, which collapses to leave a stack that is later reduced to a stump.

questions.q: On a discordant coastline, why do headlands and bays form?
options: Bands of hard and soft rock lie parallel to the coast
Bands of hard and soft rock lie at right angles to the coast, with softer rock eroding faster to form bays
The coastline is made entirely of resistant granite
Deposition builds out the harder rock into headlands
questions.explain: Where alternating rock bands meet the coast at right angles, the less resistant rock erodes faster to form bays, leaving the resistant rock as headlands.

questions.q: Which process best describes freeze-thaw weathering?
options: Rainwater chemically dissolves minerals in the rock
Water enters cracks, freezes and expands, repeatedly widening the cracks until the rock breaks
Plant roots grow into the rock and split it apart
Waves compress air in cracks, weakening the rock
questions.explain: Freeze-thaw (mechanical weathering) works because water expands by about 9% when it freezes, prising cracks apart over repeated cycles.

questions.q: Which of the following defines hydraulic action?
options: Rocks carried by waves are thrown against the cliff, wearing it away
The force of water and compressed air being forced into cracks in the rock
Rocks colliding with one another and becoming smaller and rounder
Weak acids in seawater dissolving rock such as limestone
questions.explain: Hydraulic action is the erosive force of breaking waves compressing air within cracks, gradually weakening and breaking the rock.

questions.q: The process of attrition results in which of the following?
options: Cliffs being undercut at their base
Rock fragments becoming smaller, smoother and rounder as they collide
Dissolved material being carried in the water
Sediment being deposited to form a beach
questions.explain: Attrition is the collision of transported rock particles with each other, gradually reducing their size and rounding them.

questions.q: How does a wave-cut platform form?
options: Sediment is deposited at the base of a cliff during storms
A wave-cut notch is eroded at the cliff base, the cliff is undercut and collapses, and this repeats as the cliff retreats
A river deposits material as it enters the sea
Longshore drift moves shingle to form a flat surface
questions.explain: Repeated erosion of a notch undercuts the cliff, causing collapse and cliff retreat, leaving a gently sloping rocky platform exposed at low tide.

questions.q: Why does a spit often develop a curved (recurved) end?
options: Rivers push the sediment back towards the land
A change in the prevailing wind or wave direction curves the deposited material landwards
The sea wall blocks further growth
Deposition only occurs at high tide
questions.explain: A spit grows by longshore drift across a bay or estuary, and a change in wind or wave direction curves its end round to form a recurved (hooked) end.

questions.q: Groynes are an example of which management strategy, and how do they work?
options: Soft engineering that adds sand to widen the beach
Hard engineering; wooden or rock barriers built at right angles to the beach to trap sediment moved by longshore drift
Soft engineering that allows the sea to flood low-value land
Hard engineering; a concrete barrier built along the base of a cliff
questions.explain: Groynes are a hard-engineering method that traps sediment being moved along the coast by longshore drift, building up a wider protective beach.

questions.q: Which of the following is a soft-engineering approach to coastal management?
options: Building a sea wall
Beach nourishment (adding sand or shingle to a beach)
Placing rock armour (rip-rap) at the cliff base
Constructing gabions
questions.explain: Beach nourishment is soft engineering because it works with natural processes by replacing sediment rather than building large artificial structures.

questions.q: Which set of characteristics is typical of the upper course of a river?
options: Wide, deep channel with a gentle gradient and large floodplain
Narrow, shallow channel with a steep gradient, vertical erosion and large angular bedload
Very wide channel with deposition forming a delta
Slow-flowing channel dominated by lateral erosion
questions.explain: In the upper course the steep gradient drives vertical erosion, producing a narrow, shallow channel carrying large, angular material.

questions.q: How does a waterfall lead to the formation of a gorge?
options: Deposition builds up rock at the base of the waterfall
Softer rock is eroded and undercuts the harder cap rock, which collapses and causes the waterfall to retreat upstream, leaving a gorge
Lateral erosion widens the valley into a gorge
The river deposits material as it plunges over the edge
questions.explain: As softer rock beneath the resistant cap is eroded and the plunge pool undercuts it, the overhang collapses and the waterfall retreats, leaving a steep-sided gorge.

questions.q: At a meander, where is erosion greatest and what landform does it produce?
options: On the inner bank, forming a river cliff
On the outer bank where flow is fastest, forming a river cliff
On the inner bank where flow is slowest, forming a slip-off slope
In the centre of the channel, forming a levee
questions.explain: The fastest flow (thalweg) hits the outer bank, causing erosion and a steep river cliff, while slower water on the inner bank deposits a slip-off slope.

questions.q: How is an ox-bow lake formed?
options: A meander neck is narrowed by erosion until the river cuts across it, and deposition then seals off the old loop
A river deposits sediment to build a horseshoe-shaped bank
A waterfall retreats and leaves a circular lake
A tributary joins the main river and forms a lake
questions.explain: Erosion narrows the meander neck until, often during a flood, the river breaks through and takes the shorter route, and deposition then cuts off the abandoned loop.

questions.q: How do natural levees form along a river?
options: They are built by humans to protect against flooding
During floods the river overflows, and the heaviest material is deposited first on the banks, building them up over time
They form where the river erodes vertically into its bed
They are deposits left behind when an ox-bow lake dries up
questions.explain: When a river floods, water slows on leaving the channel and drops its coarsest load nearest the banks, raising them into natural embankments (levees) over repeated floods.

questions.q: A geographer observes a river that is actively deepening its channel and cutting downwards through the landscape near its source. Which process is dominant here?
options: Lateral erosion
Vertical erosion
Deposition
Attrition
questions.explain: Downcutting into the bed, typical of the steep upper course near the source, is vertical erosion, which helps create V-shaped valleys.

questions.q: A stretch of coast is losing its beach because sediment is being carried away, and a nearby town wants a low-cost method that works with natural processes. Which option best fits?
options: Building a large concrete sea wall along the whole frontage
Beach nourishment combined with managed retreat of low-value land
Installing continuous rock armour at every cliff base
Dredging the seabed offshore
questions.explain: Beach nourishment and managed retreat are soft-engineering options that are generally cheaper and work with natural processes rather than against them.

questions.q: A student is shown a UK landscape with high rugged relief, thin soils and exposed resistant rock with few settlements. Which type of landscape is this most likely to be?
options: A lowland landscape
An upland landscape
A coastal depositional landscape
A river floodplain
questions.explain: Upland landscapes in the UK are characterised by high, rugged relief, resistant rock, thin soils and sparse settlement.

questions.q: A river in its lower course regularly floods a wide, flat area, leaving behind a layer of fine fertile sediment. What is this feature and deposited material called?
options: A gorge covered in scree
A floodplain covered in alluvium
An interlocking spur covered in bedload
A wave-cut platform covered in shingle
questions.explain: The wide, flat area either side of a lower-course river is a floodplain, built up by deposits of fine fertile sediment called alluvium during floods.

specSource: Eduqas GCSE Geography A specification; Landscapes and Physical Processes
